source_document.title: Starting Strength: Basic Barbell Training - The Squat
source_document.author: Mark Rippetoe

global_issues.title: Non-Sagittal (Side-View) Angle Detected
global_issues.message: The video was recorded from a frontal, angled, or non-sagittal perspective. In Starting Strength (Ref p. 2 Fig 2-1 & Ref p. 8 Fig 2-5), squat depth, bar-path verticality, and back inclination are strictly defined in the sagittal plane. In a frontal projection, depth cannot be validated because the femur is foreshortened. Camera must be positioned 90 degrees directly to the side of the lifter at hip height.
global_issues.actionable_cue: Relocate camera to a pure side-view perpendicular to the lifter's stance.

findings.source_citation: Ref p. 2, Fig 2-1; Ref p. 15; Ref p. 16, Fig 2-10; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 5, 18, 19, 38)

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: The hip joint, as identified by the apex in the crease of the shorts (B), must drop below the top of the patella (A). The plane formed by these two points must drop below parallel with the ground. Full depth ensures hamstring/glute/adductor recruitment and balances anterior quadriceps forces.

findings.explanation: Cannot assess sagittal planar biomechanics from a frontal or off-angle view. Plane between hip crease and patella cannot be resolved.
findings.actionable_feedback: Record from a 90° perpendicular side view at hip height.
findings.uncertainty_and_limitations: Camera perspective violation prevents planar measurement.

findings.source_citation: Ref p. 6; Ref p. 8, Fig 2-5; Ref p. 9, Fig 2-6; Ref p. 11, Fig 2-7; Ref p. 32, Fig 2-22 (PDF pp. 9, 11, 12, 14, 35)

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: Gravity operates straight down in a vertical line perpendicular to the earth. The most efficient bar path is a straight vertical line directly over the balance point: the midfoot (halfway between either end of the sole of the shoe). Horizontal deviation creates wasteful moment arms and rotational effort.

findings.actionable_feedback: Record from a 90° perpendicular side view at hip height.
findings.uncertainty_and_limitations: Camera perspective violation prevents planar measurement.

findings.criterion_name: Back Angle at Bottom (~45° Inclined / Non-Vertical)
findings.source_section: Figure 2-5, Figure 2-13 & The Important Things You're Going to Do Wrong
findings.source_citation: Ref p. 9, Fig 2-5; Ref p. 12; Ref p. 22, Fig 2-13; Ref p. 32, Fig 2-22; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 12, 15, 25, 35, 38)

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: In the low-bar back squat, the back must be inclined at approximately a 45-degree angle relative to the floor at the bottom of the squat, NOT vertical. A vertical back angle fails to load the hamstrings and pushes knees too far forward; an excessively horizontal angle indicates back rounding or chest collapse.

findings.explanation: Cannot assess sagittal planar biomechanics from a frontal or off-angle view. Plane between hip crease and patella cannot be resolved.
findings.actionable_feedback: Record from a 90° perpendicular side view at hip height.
findings.uncertainty_and_limitations: Camera perspective violation prevents planar measurement.

findings.criterion_name: Hip Drive Initiation out of Bottom
findings.source_citation: Ref p. 1; Ref p. 22, Fig 2-14; Ref p. 23; Ref p. 32, Fig 2-22; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 4, 25, 26, 35, 38)

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: Ascent out of the bottom must be driven by shoving the hips straight up ('butt straight up in the air, not forward'). The lifter must NOT lead the ascent by raising the chest, nor push the knees forward, which slackens the hamstrings and kills hip drive.

findings.explanation: Cannot assess sagittal planar biomechanics from a frontal or off-angle view. Plane between hip crease and patella cannot be resolved.
findings.actionable_feedback: Record from a 90° perpendicular side view at hip height.
findings.uncertainty_and_limitations: Camera perspective violation prevents planar measurement.

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: Eyes must be directed downward at a point on the floor 4 to 5 feet in front of the lifter with chin down, maintaining neutral anatomical cervical spine position. Looking up at the ceiling slacks the hamstrings, pulls knees/hips forward, and puts the loaded neck into unsafe hyperextension.

findings.actionable_feedback: Record from a 90° perpendicular side view at hip height.
findings.uncertainty_and_limitations: Camera perspective violation prevents planar measurement.

findings.source_citation: Ref p. 22, Fig 2-13; Ref p. 32, Fig 2-22; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 25, 35, 38)

supporting_evidence.standard_benchmark: At the bottom of the squat, knees should be just a little in front of the toes, with femurs tracking outward. Knees should reach their forward position early in descent and remain stable rather than sliding forward late.

session_summary.headline: Recording Unsuitable for Complete Biomechanical Assessment
session_summary.primary_coaching_cue: Relocate camera to a pure side-view perpendicular to the lifter's stance.

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.citation: Ref p. 14; Ref p. 20, Fig 2-12; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 17, 23, 38)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: Heels should be approximately shoulder-width apart. Excessively wide stance causes adductors to reach end of extensibility early; excessive narrowness jams thighs against the belly. Both prevent proper depth.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: CANNOT ASSESS FROM 2D SAGITTAL SIDE VIEW. Heel-to-heel lateral spacing requires a frontal, rear, or top-down camera angle. In a pure side view, the lateral dimension is compressed to zero depth. Per Starting Strength Ref p. 14, verify stance width with a front/rear camera check.

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.citation: Ref p. 14; Ref p. 20, Fig 2-12; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 17, 23, 38)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: Toes should point outward at approximately 30 degrees to match the femur angle and allow knees to track properly.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: CANNOT ASSESS FROM 2D SAGITTAL SIDE VIEW. Horizontal 30-degree toe flair requires an overhead or frontal camera view. Side-view projection collapses foot rotation. Ref p. 14 recommends looking down at your feet before unracking.

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.criterion_name: Knees Shoved Out / Thighs Parallel to Feet
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.citation: Ref p. 14; Ref p. 22, Fig 2-13; Ref p. 33; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 17, 25, 36, 38)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: Knees must be actively shoved outward during descent so femurs track parallel to feet, engaging adductors and external rotators. Lateral knee cave (valgus) diminishes hip drive and causes high squats.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: CANNOT ASSESS FROM 2D SAGITTAL SIDE VIEW. Lateral knee tracking occurs in the frontal plane. From the side, the closer leg occludes the far leg and lateral knee cave cannot be distinguished from sagittal knee travel. Ref p. 33 notes if depth is high, actively shove knees out.

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.criterion_name: Grip & Wrist Alignment (Thumbs on top, straight wrists)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: Thumbs placed on top of bar, wrists straight with forearms, elbows lifted to trap bar against back. Prevents wrist/elbow pain from carrying load on arms.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: CANNOT ASSESS FROM SIDE VIEW. Standard barbell plates and shoulders occlude hands and wrists in sagittal profile. Thumbs on top and straight wrist alignment should be checked during rack setup (Ref p. 28).

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.citation: Ref p. 13, Fig 2-8; Ref p. 29, Fig 2-19, Fig 2-20; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 16, 32, 38)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: The bar should rest in the lowest secure position on the back: directly below the spine of the scapula on the shelf formed by the posterior deltoids. If placed high on the traps (high-bar), it forces a vertical torso and knee-dominant mechanics.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: Bar placement cannot be definitively confirmed from side view: standard 45lb/20kg bumper plates occlude the lifter's upper back and scapular spine. In accordance with assignment instructions, unassessable result reported rather than invented precision.

non_assessable_side_view_criteria.citation: Ref p. 26; Ref p. 30, Fig 2-21; Ref p. 33; Ref p. 35 (PDF pp. 29, 33, 36, 38)
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.standard_description: Rack height set at mid-sternum. Lifter steps back out of the rack with 1 step, both feet under bar, tight chest/back. Never step backward to rack.
non_assessable_side_view_criteria.explanation: CANNOT ASSESS: Video starts with lifter already in position or rack uprights are outside the camera frame.
